questions.q: What is meant by 'feys&tqys iz;ksx' (mixed usage) of Hindi, Urdu, and folk language in the context of this poem? Give one example from the text.
questions.a: Mixed usage refers to the deliberate blending of words and grammatical forms from Hindi (Sanskrit-derived), Urdu (Persian/Arabic-derived), and local folk dialects within the same text. For example, the poem uses "yksdk nsuk" (folk) alongside "HkkSfrd" (Sanskrit/Hindi) and "izeq[k" (Urdu). A wrong answer that only lists words without identifying their language origin shows the student cannot distinguish the linguistic layers.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet might choose the folk expression "yksdk nsuk" over the standard Hindi "pyar karna" in the line "yksdk nsuk] ?kqVfu;ksa esa ysdj diM+s fiUgkuk".
questions.a: The folk expression "yksdk nsuk" carries the raw, earthy intimacy of village life, evoking the physical act of carrying a child on the hip while working, which "pyar karna" (an abstract, formal term) cannot capture. A wrong answer that says "they mean the same thing" misses the connotative and cultural weight of the folk phrase.

questions.q: In the line "j{kkcaèku dh lqcg jl dh iqryh", identify the grammatical construction of "j{kkcaèku" and "lqcg". How does the compound word formation contribute to the imagery?
questions.a: "j{kkcaèku" is a tatpurusha compound (j{kk + caèku) meaning 'kitchen', and "lqcg" is a bahuvrihi compound (lq + cg) meaning 'having good limbs' or 'beautiful'. The compounds compress whole images into single words, making the description dense and vivid. A wrong answer that parses them as separate words fails to see the economy and imagery of compounding.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poet's use of the feminine rhyme scheme (e.g., "gw¡/vkrh gS", "NsM+ks/uhan vkrh gS") in creating a musical quality that suits the poem's theme. Support your evaluation with evidence.

A wrong answer that calls it "just rhyming" ignores the connection between sound and sense.
